question.en: Explain a RAG pipeline and the main ways it can fail.

answer.en: Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant external content for a query, places selected evidence into the model context, and asks the model to answer using that grounding. Failures can occur before generation: parsing or chunking loses meaning, indexing is stale, the query does not match the representation, access control is missing, or retrieval returns irrelevant or incomplete passages. Generation can then misread evidence, overstate certainty, or answer beyond it. Evaluate retrieval and answer quality separately, preserve document permissions and provenance, and make “not enough evidence” a valid outcome. RAG improves access to evidence; it does not guarantee truth.

question.en: How would you decide between RAG, prompting, and fine-tuning for a product requirement?

answer.en: Use prompting for instructions, format, and task behavior; use RAG when the answer depends on changing, private, or source-attributed information; consider fine-tuning when a stable behavior or style is repeatedly required and you have suitable training data. These choices are not mutually exclusive. First define the failure and measure a baseline with a representative evaluation set. RAG cannot repair a reasoning or policy problem, and fine-tuning is not a substitute for current facts or authorization. Prefer the least complex intervention that improves the measured requirement, while accounting for maintenance, privacy, latency, cost, and rollback.

question.en: Vector RAG was the first attempt at grounding a model in company data. What other ways do you have?

answer.en: A knowledge graph when relationships between entities matter more than similarity. A semantic layer over structured data when the question is really a query. Direct tool calls to internal APIs. Hybrid retrieval that combines keyword and vector search with re-ranking. And the unglamorous part: pipelines that turn text, PDF, HTML and images into readable chunks and keep the index up to date. The design question is what goes in the prompt and what the model retrieves or queries by itself, because every option trades latency, freshness and maintenance differently.

question.en: When would you NOT use RAG?

answer.en: When the data is structured and queryable, answer with a SQL query or a tool call instead of retrieving text. When everything relevant fits reliably in the context window, just put it there. When the task is style or format adaptation at scale, fine-tuning or a strong system prompt beats retrieval. When freshness is the only problem, a scheduled prompt update or cache invalidation may be enough. RAG adds a pipeline to maintain (chunking, indexing, freshness) plus retrieval latency and cost, so if the failure mode it fixes is not present, it is over-engineering. The interviewer is listening for trade-off fluency: retrieval speed against context length, and prompting against fine-tuning.

question.en: When is putting the whole knowledge base in the prompt better than building RAG?

answer.en: Size decides the simple case: if the corpus fits comfortably in the context window, put it there. Anthropic's rule of thumb is that a knowledge base under about 200K tokens can go straight into the prompt, and prompt caching makes repeated calls cheap and fast because the stable prefix is processed once. Long context stops working when the corpus keeps growing, when different users may see different documents, when freshness matters more than convenience, or when you need per-claim attribution: those are retrieval jobs, and access control must be enforced at retrieval time, not by asking the model to ignore things. The latency cost of a long prompt is also smaller than people assume — generation dominates — but input cost still scales per request. Measure both designs on the same eval set before committing.

question.en: When does hybrid search with a reranker pay off, and when is plain vector search enough?

answer.en: Plain vector search misses exact matches: identifiers, error codes, product SKUs. If queries contain those, add a lexical layer (BM25) and fuse the rankings; in Anthropic’s experiments, hybrid retrieval over contextualized chunks cut the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 49%. A reranker then scores the top candidates against the query and keeps the best few — the same setup with reranking cut failures by 67%, and sending fewer, better chunks to the model often pays for the extra step. But reranking is runtime work: scoring more candidates buys recall and adds latency and cost, so tune the top-N on your own eval set. For a small corpus with purely semantic queries, plain vector search is usually enough; add layers only when measured retrieval failures justify them.

question.en: How do you keep a RAG index from serving stale content or content the requester should not see?

answer.en: Treat the index as a cache of the source of truth, never as the truth itself. Freshness: re-index incrementally when sources change, carry document timestamps and validity into the chunks, invalidate on edit or deletion, and make 'the answer is not in the index yet' a valid outcome. Permissions: filter by document ACL at query time, before ranking, keep tenant boundaries inside the index, and never delegate visibility to the model — retrieval must return only what the requester may see, because anything in context can leak or influence the answer. Test both sides: retrieval evals where the right answer is missing, outdated, or forbidden, so a regression in indexing or filtering fails in CI instead of in production.

question.en: What does a semantic layer add on top of a warehouse, and where does dbt fit?

answer.en: A semantic layer declares business entities, dimensions and metrics once — revenue, active customer, conversion — so BI tools, applications and AI agents query the same definitions instead of re-deriving them per tool. For a model or agent it turns a structured question into a governed query instead of retrieved prose: grounding for numbers. dbt's MetricFlow is the definition layer on top of dbt models: semantic models declare entities, dimensions and time, metrics compose (simple, ratio, derived, cumulative) and joins are inferred from entity types instead of hand-written per query. It earns its place when several consumers must agree on the same number; it is overhead for a single dashboard. The failure it prevents is metric drift: five tools, five different revenues.
